paragraphs.paraphrase: The god Hermes calls up the ghosts of the dead suitors with his golden wand (the one that puts people to sleep or wakes them) and leads them down to the land of the dead. They follow him squeaking and gibbering, like bats shrieking round a cave when one drops from the hanging cluster. They pass Oceanus, the rock Leucas, the gates of the sun and the land of dreams, and reach the meadow of asphodel where the dead live.

barriers.quote: Then Hermes of Cyllene summoned the ghosts of the suitors
barriers.my_reading: The story jumps without warning from Odysseus leaving town to the underworld. Hermes is apparently the god who guides the dead; 'of Cyllene' is an unexplained place title.

barriers.quote: the waters of Oceanus and the rock Leucas, they came to the gates of the sun and the land of dreams
barriers.my_reading: Mythical landmarks on the road to the land of the dead at the edge of the world. None is explained, but the gist (a journey beyond the living world) is clear.

barriers.quote: the meadow of asphodel
barriers.my_reading: A field of (pale) flowers in the underworld where the dead dwell; 'those who can labor no more' = the dead.

paragraphs.paraphrase: There they find the ghosts of Achilles (son of Peleus), Patroclus, Antilochus and Ajax. Ajax was the finest and handsomest of the Greeks after Achilles himself.

barriers.quote: the Danaans
barriers.my_reading: Apparently the Greeks (the army at Troy). Never explained, and within a few paragraphs the same people are also called Achaeans and Argives.

barriers.quote: after Peleus’s son himself
barriers.my_reading: Achilles, introduced a line earlier as 'son of Peleus'. The text keeps switching between names and 'son of' titles.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The ghosts gather round Achilles, and Agamemnon's ghost joins them, grieving, surrounded by the ghosts of the men who died with him in Aegisthus's house. Achilles speaks first.

barriers.quote: They gathered around the ghost of Peleus’s son
barriers.my_reading: Probably the other heroes' ghosts (Patroclus, Antilochus, Ajax), not the suitors, who ¶7 says arrive only later. A reader naturally takes 'they' to be the suitors from ¶0–1 and has to go back.

barriers.quote: those who had died with him in Aegisthus’s house
barriers.my_reading: Agamemnon and his men were killed together at the house of a man named Aegisthus. ¶6 later says Aegisthus and Agamemnon's wife murdered him; at this point who Aegisthus is, and why they died there, is unexplained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Achilles tells Agamemnon they all used to say Zeus loved him above every other hero, since he commanded the army at Troy, yet death took him too soon. It would have been better to die in glory at Troy, where the Greeks would have raised a burial mound over him and his son would have inherited his fame, than to meet the wretched end he did.

barriers.quote: Son of Atreus
barriers.my_reading: Agamemnon. His father's name, Atreus, is confirmed only in ¶9 ('Agamemnon, son of Atreus').

paragraphs.paraphrase: Agamemnon replies that Achilles was the lucky one, dying at Troy far from home while the best of both armies fought around his body. There was a day-long battle over the corpse, stopped only by a storm from Zeus. The Greeks carried him to the ships, washed him and mourned, tearing their hair. His mother rose from the sea with her nymphs, wailing so loudly that the army nearly fled, until old Nestor told them it was only his mother coming to see her son.

barriers.quote: Fortunate son of Peleus,” replied Agamemnon’s ghost, “for dying at Troy
barriers.my_reading: 'You were fortunate, Achilles, to die at Troy.' The sentence is split by the speech tag and has no main verb.

barriers.quote: far from Argos
barriers.my_reading: 'Far from home': either Greece in general or Agamemnon's (or Achilles's) own kingdom. Which is meant is unclear.

barriers.quote: fighting for your body
barriers.my_reading: The two armies fought over Achilles's corpse: the Greeks to recover it, the Trojans to seize it.

barriers.quote: mighty in your might, no longer troubled about your prowess in battle
barriers.my_reading: His huge body lay sprawled in the dust; in death he no longer cared about his fighting skill.
barriers.note: 'Mighty in your might' sounds odd aloud.

barriers.quote: Hold fast, Argives, do not flee, sons of the Achaeans
barriers.my_reading: 'Argives' and 'Achaeans' both mean the Greek army here; with 'Danaans' in ¶1, that is three names for one people.

paragraphs.paraphrase: After Nestor's words the Greeks stopped being afraid. Sea-nymphs stood weeping around the body and dressed it in divine clothes, the nine Muses sang a lament that made every Greek cry, and gods and men mourned for seventeen days. On the eighteenth they burned him on a pyre with sacrifices, divine robes, ointments and honey, while warriors on foot and on horseback clashed their armor as they paraded around it. At dawn they gathered his bones, soaked them in oil and wine, and put them in a golden urn from his mother, mixed with Patroclus's bones, with Antilochus's kept separately.

barriers.quote: The daughters of the old man of the sea
barriers.my_reading: Sea goddesses, presumably the 'immortal nymphs' who came with his mother. 'The old man of the sea' is never identified.

barriers.quote: with the tramp of a great multitude
barriers.my_reading: The heavy marching footsteps of a huge crowd (not a vagrant).

barriers.quote: when the flames of heaven had done their work
barriers.my_reading: When the pyre fire (called heavenly, perhaps because the gods kindled or fanned it) had burned out. Could be misread as lightning.

barriers.quote: a gift from Dionysus and the work of Hephaestus himself
barriers.my_reading: A divine urn, made by a craftsman god (Hephaestus) and given by Dionysus. Neither god's role is explained.
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only: Hephaestus = smith god, Dionysus = wine god.

barriers.quote: separately we enclosed those of Antilochus
barriers.my_reading: Antilochus's bones were kept apart, though buried in the same place. Whether in the same urn or another container is unclear.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The army built a great tomb over the bones on a headland above the Hellespont, visible from far out at sea to all future generations. His mother Thetis got splendid prizes from the gods for funeral games among the best Greeks, finer than at any hero's funeral, so Achilles's fame lives forever. Agamemnon contrasts his own fate: after the war, Zeus let him be murdered on his return by Aegisthus and his own wicked wife.

barriers.quote: the open Hellespont
barriers.my_reading: A stretch of sea, apparently near Troy.

barriers.quote: when young men gird themselves
barriers.my_reading: 'Gird themselves' = get ready, belt up for athletic contests. The custom of holding sports contests at a funeral is implied rather than explained.

barriers.quote: silver-footed Thetis
barriers.my_reading: Achilles's mother, the sea goddess, named here for the first time, with a traditional descriptive title.

barriers.quote: at the hands of Aegisthus and my wicked wife
barriers.my_reading: He was murdered on his homecoming by Aegisthus together with his own wife. What linked Aegisthus to his wife isn't said.
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only: Aegisthus was her lover.

paragraphs.paraphrase: While they talk, Hermes arrives with the ghosts of the suitors Odysseus killed. Astonished, the ghosts of Agamemnon and Achilles go straight up to them. Agamemnon recognizes Amphimedon, son of Melaneus, an Ithacan who had once been his host, and speaks to him.

barriers.quote: presently Hermes came up to them with the ghosts of the suitors
barriers.my_reading: The suitors only arrive now, so ¶1's 'Here they found the ghost of Achilles' either jumped ahead or meant someone else. The order of events in ¶0–7 is muddled. ('Presently' = soon after.)

paragraphs.paraphrase: Agamemnon asks Amphimedon what brought so many fine young men, all the same age, down to the dead: a storm at sea sent by Poseidon, or enemies on land while they were stealing cattle and sheep, or in a battle over a city and its women? He reminds Amphimedon that he once stayed at his house when he and Menelaus came to recruit Odysseus for the war against Troy, and it took a whole month to persuade him.

barriers.quote: all of an age too
barriers.my_reading: All the same age.

barriers.quote: cattle-lifting
barriers.my_reading: Stealing cattle (rustling).

barriers.quote: or fighting to defend their wives and city
barriers.my_reading: 'Their' seems to mean the enemies, defending their own wives and city against the young men's raid. It can also be read as the suitors defending their own wives and city.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Amphimedon agrees to tell everything. With Odysseus long gone, the suitors courted Penelope, who neither refused nor agreed to marry, secretly planning their ruin. Her trick: she started a huge piece of cloth and asked them to wait until she finished a burial shroud for Laertes, so the local women wouldn't gossip about a rich man being buried without one. She worked on it by day and undid it by torchlight at night, fooling them for three years, until in the fourth a maid told them and they caught her unpicking it. She had to finish it, and the finished cloth shone like the sun or moon.

barriers.quote: Sweethearts
barriers.my_reading: Her way of addressing the suitors. It sounds flirtatious and oddly modern, at odds with her faithfulness, unless it is meant as fake sweetness, as told by a resentful suitor.

barriers.quote: for I would not have my skill in needlework perish unrecorded
barriers.my_reading: She doesn't want her work wasted, or wants something to show for her skill. The phrase doesn't connect clearly with her request to wait.

barriers.quote: a pall for the hero Laertes
barriers.my_reading: A burial cloth (shroud) for Laertes, Odysseus's elderly father; he is only identified as Odysseus's father later (¶11–12). 'Pall' and 'laid out' (prepared for burial) are unfamiliar.
barriers.note: 'Pall' today mostly means a gloomy atmosphere.

barriers.quote: her great web
barriers.my_reading: The large piece of cloth she was making, not a spider's web. The object shifts from embroidery frame/needlework/stitches to 'web' to 'pall' to 'robe', so it is unclear whether she is weaving or embroidering, and what the thing is.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Amphimedon continues: some hostile god brought Odysseus to his swineherd's farm, where Telemachus joined him from a voyage to Pylos, and they plotted together. Odysseus came to town disguised as a ragged old beggar; no one recognized him, and the suitors insulted and pelted him while he silently put up with it. Prompted by Zeus, he and Telemachus hid the weapons in a locked inner room, and Odysseus had Penelope set up a contest with his bow and some iron. No suitor could even string the bow; despite their protests Telemachus made sure Odysseus got it, and he strung it easily and shot through the iron. Then he shot Antinous first and the others after, with a god helping his side, until the floor ran with blood. Their bodies still lie unwashed and unmourned because their families don't yet know.

barriers.quote: offer his bow and a quantity of iron to be competed for
barriers.my_reading: A contest to string Odysseus's bow and shoot through some iron objects. 'A quantity of iron' reads like a prize, and then 'sent his arrow through the iron' makes no sense.
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only: the arrow went through a row of axe-heads.

barriers.quote: aegis-bearing Zeus
barriers.my_reading: A traditional title for Zeus; the aegis seems to be some shield or emblem of his. The modern phrase 'under the aegis of' doesn't help.

barriers.quote: took the weapons and hid them in an inner room
barriers.my_reading: They removed the weapons kept in the hall so the suitors would be unarmed for the fight. Which weapons, and why, is left to inference.

barriers.quote: stood on the floor of the gallery and poured his arrows on the ground
barriers.my_reading: He took a position in the hall ('gallery') and tipped the arrows out of his quiver at his feet so he could shoot fast. 'Stood on the floor' is odd, since everyone was on the floor.

barriers.quote: for they fell upon us with might and main
barriers.my_reading: 'They' = Odysseus, Telemachus and their helpers, although only Odysseus has been mentioned shooting. 'With might and main' = with all their strength.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Agamemnon, speaking to the absent Odysseus, calls him lucky to have such a wise and faithful wife as Penelope, daughter of Icarius: her virtue will be famous forever, and the gods will make a song in her honor. By contrast, the daughter of Tyndareus, who murdered her husband, will be the subject of a hateful song that shames all women, even good ones.

barriers.quote: Fortunate Odysseus, son of Laertes,” replied Agamemnon’s ghost
barriers.my_reading: Agamemnon is answering Amphimedon but exclaims to Odysseus, who isn't there. A reader may briefly think Odysseus is present.

barriers.quote: the daughter of Tyndareus, who killed her lawful husband
barriers.my_reading: Agamemnon's own wife, the 'wicked wife' of ¶6, who murdered him. She is never named, and the reader has to connect this to ¶6.

paragraphs.paraphrase: While the dead talk in the underworld, Odysseus and his companions leave town and reach Laertes's well-farmed country estate, which he had brought into cultivation with endless work. His house has a lean-to all around it where his slaves eat, sit and sleep, and inside an old Sicel woman looks after him. Odysseus speaks to his son and the two herdsmen.

barriers.quote: which he had reclaimed with endless labor
barriers.my_reading: He had turned wild or waste land into farmland by his own hard work. 'Reclaimed' could be read as 'got back'.

barriers.quote: a lean-to running all around it
barriers.my_reading: A shed-like annex or covered structure built against the house on all sides, used as quarters for the slaves.

barriers.quote: an old Sicel woman
barriers.my_reading: A woman of the Sicels, apparently a foreign people (perhaps from Sicily). Never explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: He tells them to go into the house and kill the best pig for dinner, while he sees whether his father will recognize him after so long.

Odysseus hands his armor to Eumaeus and Philoetius, who go on to the house, and walks down into the vineyard and orchard to test his father. Dolius, his sons and the other slaves are away gathering thorns for a hedge, so he finds Laertes alone, hoeing round a vine, in a filthy patched tunic, leather leg-wrappings and sleeves against the brambles, and a goatskin cap, looking grief-stricken. Odysseus weeps under a pear tree, torn between embracing him at once and questioning him first, and decides to try a trick on him.

barriers.quote: he did not see Dolius, nor any of his sons nor the other bondservants
barriers.my_reading: Dolius is apparently an old servant of Laertes with several sons (explained only in ¶25). 'Bondservants' = slaves or bound laborers.

barriers.quote: at the place where the old man had told them
barriers.my_reading: Probably Laertes, the master giving orders, but 'the old man' could just as well be Dolius.

barriers.quote: bound round with thongs of oxhide
barriers.my_reading: Strips of cowhide leather wrapped round his shins as leggings.

barriers.quote: He doubted whether to embrace him
barriers.my_reading: 'Doubted whether' = couldn't decide whether (old usage).

paragraphs.paraphrase: Posing as a stranger, Odysseus praises the old man's gardening (every plant shows his care) but says he neglects himself: he is old, unkempt and ragged, yet looks nobly born rather than like a slave, and ought to be living in comfort. He asks whose slave he is and whether this is really Ithaca, since a surly man he met wouldn't hear him out. Then he spins a story: he once hosted a dear friend from Ithaca, son of Laertes son of Arceisius, and sent him off with lavish gifts: seven talents of gold, a flower-engraved silver cup, many cloaks, tapestries, rugs, mantles and shirts, and four skilled slave women of his choosing.

barriers.quote: There is not a single plant, not a fig tree, vine, olive, pear, nor flower bed, but bears the trace of your attention
barriers.my_reading: Every plant shows your care. The 'not a single ... but' construction can be misread as 'no plant shows your care'.

barriers.quote: It cannot be because you are idle that your master takes such poor care of you
barriers.my_reading: Odysseus pretends to take his father for a slave and says his master's neglect can't be a punishment for laziness, given how well he works.

barriers.quote: his father was Laertes, son of Arceisius
barriers.my_reading: The 'old friend' is Odysseus himself, and Arceisius is Laertes's father. So he is telling his own father an invented story about having hosted his son.
barriers.note: The reader must remember 'be crafty' in ¶14 to see this is a deception; nothing flags it.

barriers.quote: seven talents of fine gold
barriers.my_reading: 'Talent' here is a unit of weight for gold, not an ability.

barriers.quote: twelve cloaks of single fold, twelve rugs, twelve fair mantles
barriers.my_reading: Unlined, single-layer cloaks; 'mantles' are also cloaks. The list of near-identical garments (light cloaks, single-fold cloaks, mantles) is hard to tell apart.

barriers.quote: four good-looking women skilled in all useful arts, and I let him take his choice
barriers.my_reading: He gave four enslaved women as part of the gift and let his guest choose which ones.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Weeping, Laertes confirms this is Ithaca but says it is in the hands of wicked men, so the stranger's gifts were wasted; had his friend been alive he would have repaid them generously. He asks how long ago the stranger hosted this guest, his own unlucky son, surely dead far from home, eaten by fish or by birds and beasts, and never buried or mourned by his parents or by his wife Penelope. Then he asks who the stranger is, where he comes from, and where his ship and crew are, or whether others brought him and left.

barriers.quote: my unhappy son, if ever there was one
barriers.my_reading: 'My son, the unluckiest man who ever lived.' It can also be heard as doubt about whether he ever had a son.

barriers.quote: his excellent and richly dowered wife
barriers.my_reading: A wife who brought (or was won with) great wealth; a highly prized match.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus claims, 'truthfully', to be Eperitus from Alybas, son of King Apheidas son of Polypemon, blown off course from Sicania against his will, with his ship anchored off the countryside outside town. He says it is five years since Odysseus left his country, and that the omens were good then (birds on their right), so both hoped to meet again and exchange gifts.

barriers.quote: quite truthfully
barriers.my_reading: Everything that follows (Alybas, Apheidas, the name Eperitus) is invented as part of the test, even though he calls it truthful and the text never flags it as a lie.

barriers.quote: The birds all flew on our right hands
barriers.my_reading: Birds seen on the right were taken as a lucky omen; the text implies this with 'the omens were good'.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Laertes is overwhelmed with grief: he scoops up dust in both hands and pours it over his gray head, groaning. Deeply moved, nostrils quivering, Odysseus rushes to him, embraces and kisses him. He is the son Laertes was asking about, back after twenty years, but there's no time for tears, because he has just killed the suitors for their crimes.

barriers.quote: He filled both hands with dust from the ground and poured it over his gray head
barriers.my_reading: Pouring dust on one's head is a traditional gesture of mourning.

barriers.quote: his nostrils quivered
barriers.my_reading: A physical sign of overwhelming emotion welling up, like the sting before tears.
barriers.note: An odd image for a modern reader.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Laertes says that if this really is his son Odysseus, he needs clear proof.

Odysseus shows him the scar from a boar's tusk that he got hunting on Mount Parnassus, when his parents sent him to his mother's father Autolycus to collect promised gifts. He also recalls following Laertes round the orchard, asking about every tree, and being given thirteen pear trees, ten apple trees and forty fig trees, plus the promise of fifty rows of vines, with grain between the rows, that ripen with every kind of grape in the summer heat.

barriers.quote: as I followed you around the garden
barriers.my_reading: A memory from childhood, when as a small boy he followed his father and was promised the trees. The text doesn't actually say he was a child.

barriers.quote: with corn planted between each row
barriers.my_reading: Grain (wheat or barley). American readers will picture maize, which is out of place here.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The proofs make Laertes go weak; he clings to his son, who holds him up so he doesn't faint. When he recovers, he cries out to Zeus that the gods must still be on Olympus after all if the suitors have been punished, but he fears the whole town will soon come after them and send for help to the cities of the Cephallenians.

barriers.quote: then you gods are still on Olympus after all
barriers.my_reading: The suitors' punishment proves the gods still exist and still uphold justice; Olympus is the gods' home.

barriers.quote: throughout the cities of the Cephallenians
barriers.my_reading: The neighboring towns and islands of Odysseus's wider realm, whose people might join the avengers. Who the Cephallenians are is never explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus reassures him and suggests they go into the house by the garden, where he has sent Telemachus, Philoetius and Eumaeus to get dinner ready.

They go to the house and find Telemachus and the two herdsmen carving meat and mixing wine with water. The old Sicel woman bathes Laertes, rubs him with oil and dresses him in a fine cloak, and Athena makes him taller and sturdier. When he comes out, Odysseus is amazed at how godlike he looks and tells him some god has made him taller and handsomer.

barriers.quote: the stockman and the swineherd
barriers.my_reading: The two herdsmen, presumably Philoetius (cattle) and Eumaeus (pigs). The text never says which name goes with which job.

barriers.quote: his son was surprised to see him
barriers.my_reading: Laertes's son, i.e. Odysseus (who calls him 'father'), not Telemachus, who was mentioned just before.

barriers.quote: making him taller and stouter than before
barriers.my_reading: Sturdier and more robust, not fatter.
barriers.note: In modern English 'stout' usually means fat.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Laertes wishes, by Zeus, Athena and Apollo, that he were still the man who ruled the Cephallenians and captured the fortress of Nericum on its headland. Then he could have stood beside Odysseus in armor yesterday and killed many suitors, to his son's delight.

barriers.quote: took Nericum, that strong fortress on the foreland
barriers.my_reading: Captured a fortified town called Nericum on a headland ('foreland' = promontory).

paragraphs.paraphrase: Meanwhile the others finish preparing, take their seats and start eating. Old Dolius and his sons come in from the fields, fetched by their mother, the Sicel woman who looks after Laertes. When they recognize Odysseus they stand there stunned. Odysseus good-naturedly tells Dolius to sit down to dinner and get over his surprise, since they have been waiting to begin.

barriers.quote: their mother, the Sicel woman
barriers.my_reading: The old Sicel housekeeper is the mother of Dolius's sons, presumably Dolius's wife. This is the first time Dolius's place in the household becomes clear.

barriers.quote: We have been wanting to begin for some time and have been waiting for you.
barriers.my_reading: A friendly exaggeration or a slip: the same paragraph already said they had begun eating.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Dolius goes to Odysseus with both hands outstretched, kisses his hand at the wrist, and welcomes him home after they had given up hope, wishing him the gods' blessing. He asks whether Penelope knows yet or whether they should send someone to tell her.
Odysseus tells him Penelope already knows. Dolius's sons crowd round to greet and embrace Odysseus one after another, then sit down in order beside their father.

Meanwhile rumor spreads news of the massacre through town. People gather at Odysseus's house wailing, take away and bury their own dead, and send the bodies of men from elsewhere home on fishing boats. At an angry assembly, Eupeithes, father of Antinous (the first suitor killed), speaks through tears. Odysseus has wronged the Greeks twice: he took many good men away in his fleet and lost both ships and men, and now he has killed the leading men of the Cephallenians. They must strike before he escapes to Pylos or Elis, or they will be shamed forever; Eupeithes would rather die than leave his son unavenged.

barriers.quote: Rumor went around the town
barriers.my_reading: Rumor personified as a messenger figure; in plain terms, the news spread. The capital letter makes it look like a character's name.

barriers.quote: this man has done the Achaeans great wrong
barriers.my_reading: Eupeithes uses 'Achaeans' and, a sentence later, 'Cephallenians' for his own people: apparently Greeks in general and Odysseus's islanders. The text never explains either name or how they relate to 'men of Ithaca'.

barriers.quote: to Pylos or to Elis, where the Epeans rule
barriers.my_reading: Places across the water where Odysseus might flee; 'Epeans' is an unexplained people.

barriers.quote: Let us be up and doing
barriers.my_reading: 'Let's act now.'

paragraphs.paraphrase: Everyone pities him. Then Medon and the bard Phemius, who have woken up, arrive from Odysseus's house. To general astonishment they stand among the crowd, and Medon declares that Odysseus acted with the gods' backing: he himself saw an immortal who looked like Mentor standing by Odysseus, sometimes urging him on from in front, sometimes storming through the courtyard and cutting down the suitors.

barriers.quote: But Medon and the bard Phemius had now awakened
barriers.my_reading: Medon seems to be a member of Odysseus's household who survived the killing, like the singer Phemius. Who he is, and why the crowd is astonished to see them (presumably because they were thought dead), isn't said.

barriers.quote: take the form of Mentor
barriers.my_reading: Mentor is apparently a real Ithacan man (an elder, mentioned again in ¶31) whose appearance the god borrowed.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The people turn pale with fear, and old Halitherses, son of Mastor, the only one among them who could see both past and future, stands up to speak frankly.

Halitherses tells the Ithacans it is their own fault: they ignored him and Mentor when told to restrain their sons, who in their arrogance wasted the property and insulted the wife of a leader they assumed would never come back. He urges them not to march against Odysseus, or they will bring disaster on themselves.

barriers.quote: check the folly of your sons, who were doing much wrong in the wantonness of their hearts
barriers.my_reading: 'Check' = restrain; 'wantonness' = reckless, arrogant self-indulgence.

paragraphs.paraphrase: When he finishes, more than half the crowd shouts and leaves the assembly at once, but the rest stay, displeased with Halitherses's speech, and side with Eupeithes. These arm themselves and gather in front of the city, and Eupeithes leads them on in their folly, thinking to avenge his son, but he will die in the attempt and never come back.

barriers.quote: more than half raised a loud shout, and at once left the assembly
barriers.my_reading: As written, the majority shouted and went home (presumably heeding Halitherses), while a minority stayed, sided with Eupeithes and went to arm. But it is unclear what the shout meant, and the group that 'stayed where they were' then 'hurried off for their weapons'.
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only, and uncertain: I recall versions in which the larger group is the one that rushes to arm.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena asks Zeus, her father, whether he intends to prolong the fighting or make peace between the two sides.

Zeus replies that it was her own plan that brought Odysseus home to take revenge, so she may do as she likes. His advice: with vengeance done, both sides should swear a solemn treaty keeping Odysseus as king, while the gods make the families forgive and forget the killing of their sons and brothers, so that friendship, peace and prosperity return.

barriers.quote: while we cause the others to forgive and forget
barriers.my_reading: The gods themselves will wipe away the families' anger (a divine act of forgetting), not merely persuade them.

paragraphs.paraphrase: That is exactly what Athena wants, and she darts down from the peaks of Olympus.

After dinner at Laertes's farm, Odysseus tells someone to go out and see whether the enemy is getting close. One of Dolius's sons goes, sees from the doorway that they are already near, and calls for everyone to arm at once.

barriers.quote: see if they are not getting close up to us
barriers.my_reading: 'See whether they are getting close.' The old-style 'not' momentarily reverses the sense, and 'they' (the armed townsmen) hasn't been mentioned in the farm scene.

paragraphs.paraphrase: They arm as fast as they can: Odysseus, his three companions and Dolius's six sons, plus the gray-haired Laertes and Dolius, fighters out of necessity. Then they open the gate and march out with Odysseus in the lead.

barriers.quote: his three men
barriers.my_reading: Telemachus plus the two herdsmen, Philoetius and Eumaeus. Counting his son among 'his men' is slightly confusing.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena joins them disguised as Mentor, with his appearance and voice. Odysseus is glad to see her and tells Telemachus that in this battle, which will test every man's courage, he must not disgrace their family, famous everywhere for strength and courage.
Telemachus replies that his father is right, and that he will see Telemachus has no intention of disgracing the family.
Laertes is overjoyed: what a day, to see his son and grandson competing with each other in courage.
Athena, still disguised as Mentor, comes up to Laertes, calls him her dearest friend, and tells him to pray to Athena and to Zeus, then take aim and throw his spear.

barriers.quote: Son of Arceisius
barriers.my_reading: Laertes; his father Arceisius was mentioned only once, in ¶15. The reader has to work out that 'him' in the opening sentence is Laertes.

barriers.quote: pray to the blue-eyed maiden Athena
barriers.my_reading: Athena, disguised as Mentor, tells Laertes to pray to Athena, i.e. to herself in her true form.

barriers.quote: poise your spear and hurl it
barriers.my_reading: Balance and aim the spear in your hand, then throw it. 'Poise' usually means composure today.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Filled with new strength by Athena, Laertes prays and throws. The spear goes straight through Eupeithes's helmet and he crashes to the ground in his armor. Odysseus and Telemachus charge the enemy's front line with swords and spears and would have killed them all, but Athena shouts to the Ithacans to stop this terrible war and settle it without more bloodshed.

Terrified by the goddess's voice, the Ithacans drop their weapons and flee to the city. Odysseus gives a great war cry and swoops after them like an eagle, but Zeus hurls a fiery thunderbolt that lands just in front of Athena, and she tells Odysseus to stop fighting or Zeus will be angry with him.

barriers.quote: the son of Cronus sent a thunderbolt of fire that fell just in front of Athena
barriers.my_reading: 'Son of Cronus' = Zeus, which can only be inferred from ¶33 ('Father, son of Cronus'). The bolt landing at Athena's feet is a signal to her to end the fighting.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus gladly obeys. Athena, in Mentor's form and voice, soon makes a peace treaty between the two sides.

barriers.quote: Then Athena assumed the form and voice of Mentor
barriers.my_reading: She appears as Mentor again. She already had Mentor's form in ¶38 but spoke as a goddess in ¶42–43, so she seems to switch back to human shape to broker the treaty.

barriers.quote: presently made a covenant of peace
barriers.my_reading: 'Presently' = soon afterwards; 'covenant' = binding treaty. The Book ends abruptly without saying what the peace involves (only Zeus's speech in ¶34 hints at it).

book_level: One people, many unexplained names: Achaeans, Danaans and Argives for the Greek army (¶1–5), and later Achaeans, Cephallenians and 'men of Ithaca' for Odysseus's own people (¶21–31). A reader can't tell whether these are the same group or different ones.

People are identified by their fathers more often than by name: 'son of Peleus', 'son of Atreus', 'son of Arceisius', 'son of Cronus', 'daughter of Tyndareus'. Laertes in ¶41, Zeus in ¶43 and Agamemnon's murderous wife in ¶11 (never named) all have to be worked out from earlier paragraphs.

The underworld opening (¶0–11) assumes the reader knows the Trojan War story (Achilles, Patroclus, Antilochus, Ajax, Nestor, Thetis, Aegisthus, the Muses) and mythic geography (Oceanus, Leucas, asphodel, the Hellespont). The order of events is muddled: the suitors seem to meet Achilles in ¶1–2 but only arrive in ¶7.

Amphimedon's recap is the hardest passage: the bow contest's 'quantity of iron' and 'sent his arrow through the iron' are unintelligible without prior knowledge; the weaving trick keeps renaming its object (needlework, web, pall, robe); and 'Sweethearts' jars.

Odysseus's testing of Laertes (¶14–17) depends on the reader realizing that the 'old friend' is Odysseus himself and that the 'quite truthfully' Eperitus story is a lie; nothing in the text flags either.

Archaic words and idioms scattered throughout make it read like old English rather than modern English: presently, cattle-lifting, all of an age, gird, bondservants, thongs, doubted whether, dowered, talents, stouter, foreland, be up and doing, might and main, wantonness, poise your spear.

Minor characters appear without introduction, and their relationships come late or not at all: Dolius (his role only clear in ¶25), the Sicel woman (his wife?), Medon, Mentor, Halitherses, and which herdsman is the 'stockman' and which the 'swineherd'.

The ending is fast and confusing: the split assembly in ¶32 (which side armed?), Athena taking Mentor's form a second time, Zeus's thunderbolt landing at Athena's feet, and a peace whose terms appear only in Zeus's speech in ¶34.
